The New Zealand lesser short-tailed bat (Mystacina tuberculata) exhibits a reproductive biology constrained by its temperate habitat and the need to maintain a high and stable body temperature. Under the thermal conditions typical of an active, normothermic individual (36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]), a single female produces, at maximum, only one offspring per litter [N_R_i = one offspring per litter] and raises approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year]. This exceptionally low rate of reproduction is among the lowest recorded for any microbat, reflecting a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward adult survival and intensive maternal investment rather than high fecundity. A substantial portion of this annual cycle is dedicated to gestation, during which the gestating embryo develops for a period of 95 days [tg = 95 days] at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This extended period imposes significant energetic costs on the female, prolonging the developmental schedule relative to many other insectivorous bats. This extended gestation ultimately results in the delivery of a single, relatively well-developed neonate.

Neonatal emergence marks the beginning of an intensive period of maternal care for the newborn. At the moment of parturition, a pup is remarkably small, weighing just 4.3 grams [Wwb = 4.3 grams], a mass that represents less than thirty percent of the adult female's weight. This altricial neonate is entirely dependent on its mother for both thermoregulation and nutrition. The initial weeks of life are characterized by continuous suckling, a critical phase for the rapid accumulation of mass required for eventual flight. The mother must consume a large quantity of invertebrates daily to support the high energetic demands of milk production. This period of complete dependency on milk ingestion is sustained for a well-defined duration, with the offspring typically achieving nutritional independence at approximately 28 days after birth [tx = approximately 28 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. Weaning at this juncture marks a critical transition to solid food consumption.

The post-weaning period is a time of rapid growth and the honing of foraging skills essential for survival in the dense New Zealand forests. The suckling juvenile, now nutritionally independent, must accumulate considerable body reserves before it can reach its full adult dimensions. This phase of accelerated mass gain continues until the individual achieves its ultimate adult body mass of 14.8 grams [Wwi = 14.8 grams]. Attaining this asymptotic mass is a crucial prerequisite for the onset of reproductive competence and survival during the lean winter months. The species is known for its impressive longevity for a mammal of its small size, a trait intrinsically linked to its slow pace of life. Records from banding studies indicate that individuals can live for a maximum of approximately 7.6 years [am = approximately 7.6 years] under normothermic conditions (36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]), a lifespan that permits multiple reproductive attempts despite the annual limit of a single pup.

The journey from birth to a state of reproductive readiness is a prolonged process in this species, reflecting the complexity of sexual maturation. Young bats do not become reproductively active immediately upon achieving adult body mass; instead, sexual maturation unfolds over a much longer timeframe. In the context of the species' typical active body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], a young female will not reach puberty until around 258 days after birth [tp = around 258 days after birth]. This extended period of growth and physiological development before the first oestrus means that pups born in one breeding season are typically not ready to breed until the following year. The delay in reaching reproductive maturity is believed to be linked to the need to develop complex foraging skills and acquire sufficient fat reserves to survive hibernation and support a successful pregnancy.

This unique combination of small litter size and protracted developmental phases results in a very slow potential rate of population increase. The maximum fecundity of one offspring per litter [N_R_i = one offspring per litter] and one litter per adult female per year [F_R_i = one litter per adult female per year] at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C] is a direct outcome of the extended gestation of 95 days [tg = 95 days] and the long interval required for the individual to reach breeding condition. Compared to other temperate-zone insectivorous bats of the families Vespertilionidae and Rhinolophidae, which often produce single young but may breed more opportunistically in response to favorable conditions, the lesser short-tailed bat's reproductive output is notably constrained. Furthermore, the ability to sustain these metabolic processes relies heavily on the bat's endothermic temperature regulation. During the active season, the species typically regulates its core temperature at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], which, when combined with its modest adult body mass of 14.8 grams [Wwi = 14.8 grams], necessitates a very high mass-specific metabolic rate. This energetic constraint, coupled with the pre-weaning dependency of the young, underscores the profound vulnerability of Mystacina tuberculata to habitat degradation or the loss of large insect prey, as any disruption to its foraging success can directly impact its already limited capacity for recruitment.
